chapters.title: Chapter 5: Integrity Signals in Filings and Behaviour

lessons.title: Guidance vs Delivery: Scoring Management's Promise-Keeping

body.text: Anyone can promise. A five-year record of what management promised against what it delivered is the cheapest character test available to a retail investor.

children.text: Everything in this course so far has been about money: who holds the shares, who gets the cash, who approves the deals. This chapter is about something harder to measure and just as valuable: whether management tells you the truth about its own business. The starting point is the simplest test there is. Write down what they said they would do, then check what happened.

Most Indian companies do not give formal earnings guidance. Among large caps, the IT services sector is the main exception: Infosys publishes an annual revenue growth guidance range in constant currency and updates it every quarter, while TCS does not give formal guidance at all. Everywhere else, guidance arrives as statements on earnings calls and in investor presentations: a margin target, a capex plan, a debt reduction promise, a store opening schedule, a breakeven date. These are promises, and they are all checkable.
Where Promises Live, and Where the Answers Live

body.caption: Match each promise to the document that settles it

cells: Quarterly results and the P&L on screener.in
Purchase of fixed assets in the cash flow statement
Borrowings on the balance sheet, and net debt after cash
Use of IPO or QIP money
Objects of the issue in the prospectus or placement document
Quarterly statement of deviation or variation filed with the exchanges, and the monitoring agency report
Operating metrics in the next few presentations

body.text: The IPO promise is the most verifiable of all. Under LODR Regulation 32, a listed company must file a statement of deviation or variation in the use of issue proceeds with the exchanges every quarter, reviewed by the audit committee, and larger issues also have a monitoring agency reporting on utilisation. A company that raised money for a new plant and quietly used it for 'general corporate purposes' leaves a paper trail.

children.text: Keep one sheet per company. Every time management makes a specific, dated commitment, add a row: the date, the promise in their words, the deadline, what actually happened, and a verdict. Vague statements such as 'we remain optimistic' do not qualify. Only commitments with a number and a date go in the ledger.

body.caption: An illustrative promise ledger for one company

cells: Capex of ₹1,200 crore over two years
Net debt ₹1,900 crore; target no longer mentioned
New plant commissioned by Q2 FY25
Commissioned in Q4 FY25, explained on the concall
Exports to reach 25% of revenue by FY26
At 11% and the target has stopped appearing in presentations

body.text: The 'quietly dropped' row is the one that matters most. A missed target that management explains is a business problem. A target that simply vanishes from the investor presentation, with no one mentioning it again, is a disclosure problem. Compare the same slide across four consecutive quarterly presentations and watch what disappears.

children.text: Where a company does give numeric guidance, score it. Take an illustrative company that guided revenue growth at the start of each year and delivered the following.

stats.label: Average delivery
stats.context: An average shortfall of 4.8 percentage points

stats.label: Years met
stats.context: Counting a year as met if actual growth was within 1 point of guidance

children.text: One bad year is a business event. Four misses in five years, always in the same direction, is a pattern. Management that is consistently 5 points optimistic is not unlucky, it is either poor at forecasting its own business or willing to tell investors what they want to hear. Either way, you should discount its next forecast before putting it in a valuation.

body.title: Measure the Miss
body.prompt: At the start of the year, management guided for 18% revenue growth on a base of ₹5,000 crore. The company finished the year with revenue of ₹5,550 crore. What growth did it actually deliver? Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹5,550 crore ÷ ₹5,000 crore = 1.11, so growth was 11.0% against guidance of 18%. Guidance implied revenue of ₹5,900 crore, so the company delivered about 61% of the growth it promised. Track this ratio every year; a company that repeatedly delivers around 60% of its guided growth has told you how to read its next forecast.

children.text: Reliance Industries announced at its 2019 AGM that it aimed to become net debt free by March 2021. It got there ahead of schedule in 2020, through a huge rights issue and stake sales in Jio Platforms and its retail business rather than through operating cash flow alone. The promise was kept, and how it was kept is part of the story: existing shareholders funded a large part of it by subscribing to the rights issue. When you score a delivered promise, note the means as well as the outcome.

One 97 Communications, which runs Paytm, listed in 2021 amid heavy scepticism about when it would ever make money. Management gave a specific commitment: operating profitability, measured as EBITDA before ESOP costs, by the September 2023 quarter. It reported reaching that milestone ahead of the deadline. Whatever you think of the stock, a dated, specific, checkable promise that was met early is a mark in management's favour.

Yes Bank, in late 2019, told the market its board had received a binding offer of about US$1.2 billion from a global investor, as part of the capital raising it desperately needed. The offer was widely questioned at the time, and the money never arrived. Within months RBI had superseded the board. A promise about someone else's money, with no named, verifiable counterparty and no completed documentation, is the weakest kind of promise a company can make, and this is the moment to be most sceptical, not least.

columns.label: Honest Culture
points: Specific numbers with dates, repeated consistently across quarters
Misses acknowledged early, with reasons and a revised target
The same metrics reported every quarter, in the same format
Guidance withdrawn openly when conditions genuinely change
Bad news delivered by management before analysts find it

columns.label: Spin
points: Aspirations without deadlines, or deadlines that slide by a year every year
Targets that vanish from presentations with no comment
Metrics redefined so a miss looks like a hit, such as switching to a new adjusted profit measure
'H2 will be much better' repeated for several years
Bad news surfaced first by analysts or the media, then confirmed reluctantly

body.text: Watch for redefinition. If a company switches from reporting EBITDA to 'EBITDA before one-offs', then to 'cash EBITDA', while the target number stays the same, the goalpost moved even though the scoreboard looks unchanged. Always recompute the metric the way it was defined when the promise was made.

body.title: Read the Pattern
body.question: Over four years, a company guided for 20% revenue growth each year and delivered 12%, 11%, 13%, and 10%. Each year management explained the miss as 'a temporary demand slowdown' and guided 20% again. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The business is about to inflect, since four slow years make a recovery more likely
Management's forecasts are systematically optimistic, so its guidance should be discounted towards the delivered range before use
Guidance is irrelevant and should be ignored entirely
The misses prove the company is manipulating its accounts
body.explanation: Four misses in the same direction, with the same explanation and no change in the next forecast, is a forecasting bias, not bad luck. It does not prove any accounting problem, and it does not make guidance useless: it tells you the company's realistic growth is closer to 11% or 12%. Build your valuation on the delivered range, not the guided one.

body.title: Follow the IPO Money
body.textWithBlank: Under LODR, a listed company must file a quarterly statement of ___ or variation with the stock exchanges if it uses issue proceeds differently from the objects stated in its prospectus.
body.explanation: The statement of deviation or variation, reviewed by the audit committee, is filed with the exchanges every quarter until the issue proceeds are fully used, and many issues also have a monitoring agency reporting on utilisation. This turns an IPO promise into something you can verify rather than trust.

body.title: Three Years of H2
body.scenario: You are tracking a mid cap capital goods company on NSE. In FY24 management guided for 22% revenue growth and a 16% EBITDA margin; it delivered 9% growth and a 12.4% margin, explaining that execution was back-ended and H2 would normalise. In FY25 it guided 20% and delivered 11%, again citing back-ended execution. For FY26 it has guided 20% once more. The order book figure highlighted in every presentation has been redefined this year to include letters of intent and framework agreements. The company also raised ₹600 crore in a QIP last year for capex; the latest quarterly filing shows ₹410 crore still sitting in bank deposits and mutual funds, with the project timeline pushed out by a year.
body.prompt: How should this record change the way you read the FY26 guidance and value the company?
body.modelAnswer: Treat the 20% FY26 guidance as an aspiration worth about half its face value, because the delivered record is 9% and 11% with the same explanation both times. Three things sharpen the concern beyond ordinary forecasting error. First, the explanation has not changed across two years, so either the same mistake is being repeated or the guidance was never realistic. Second, redefining the order book to include letters of intent and framework agreements makes the headline metric non-comparable with earlier years, exactly the goalpost shift to watch for, so recompute it on the old definition before drawing conclusions. Third, ₹410 crore of the ₹600 crore QIP is unspent while the project slips, so shareholders' money is earning deposit rates instead of the returns it was raised to earn. For valuation, model 10% to 12% growth and the delivered margin rather than the guided ones, and read the quarterly statement of deviation for how the QIP money is now described. If FY26 is missed again and the order book definition changes once more, the problem has moved from optimism to disclosure quality.

body.title: Build a Promise Ledger for One Holding
steps: Download the last eight quarterly investor presentations and the last three annual reports from screener.in's Documents section
List every commitment that has a number and a date: growth, margin, capex, debt, capacity, store count, breakeven
For each, find the actual outcome in the results, cash flow statement, or balance sheet, and mark it delivered, missed, late, or quietly dropped
Put the same guidance slide from four consecutive quarters side by side and note which targets or definitions changed
If the company raised money through an IPO, QIP, or rights issue in the last three years, read the quarterly statement of deviation or variation on BSE or NSE
Calculate the hit rate and the average shortfall, then apply that discount to current guidance before using it in a valuation

body.text: Companies named in this lesson are discussed based on public disclosures, company statements, and widely reported events, for education only. The ledger and guidance figures used as illustrations are fictional. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: Formal guidance is rare in India outside IT services, but concalls and investor presentations are full of checkable, dated promises
Keep a promise ledger with date, promise, deadline, outcome, and verdict, counting delivered, missed, late, and quietly dropped separately
A target that disappears from presentations without comment is a disclosure signal, not just a business miss
Score guidance accuracy over five years; in the illustration, average guidance of 17.4% met average delivery of 12.6%, with only one year in five met
Watch for redefined metrics, such as a broadened order book or a new adjusted profit measure, which move the goalposts without moving the number
IPO and QIP promises are the most verifiable of all, through the quarterly statement of deviation or variation and the monitoring agency report
